title: Backpressure & Load Shedding
subtitle: Watch a traffic spike bury an unbounded queue, then see bounded queues, shedding and admission control keep a service alive.
learn: Why an unbounded queue turns a short spike into a long outage
How queue length converts directly into waiting time
How bounded queues and fast rejection protect latency
How to shed low-priority work first and reject at the edge
How adaptive concurrency limits track a slowing dependency

steps.title: What happens when work arrives faster than it leaves?
steps.body: Picture a service where a pool of workers finishes at most 100 requests per second. Requests wait in a queue (a line) until a worker is free. Today 80 requests per second arrive, 80% of the ceiling, so the line stays short. Every real system has a ceiling like this. The question is what it does when arrivals go above it, even briefly.
steps.idea: Every service has a maximum throughput. The design question is how it behaves beyond it.
steps.caption: Arrivals sit below capacity, so the queue stays small.

steps.title: A spike makes the queue grow
steps.body: A marketing email lands and arrivals jump to 150 requests per second. Workers still finish only 100, so 50 extra requests per second pile up in the queue. After 10 seconds the queue holds 500 requests, and a new request waits 5 seconds. A queue is a buffer that absorbs short bursts, which is useful, but only if the burst ends before the buffer fills.
steps.idea: Queue growth = arrivals minus capacity. A buffer hides overload only while it has room.
steps.caption: 150 in, 100 out: the queue grows by 50 per second.

steps.title: The unbounded queue
steps.body: Suppose the queue has no size limit. After 60 seconds of the spike it holds 3,000 requests (50 x 60). A new request waits behind all of them: 3,000 divided by 100 per second is 30 seconds. The service never returns an error. It just gets slower and slower, and memory use climbs until the process may crash.
steps.idea: Wait time = queue length divided by service rate. A long queue means a long wait for everyone.
steps.caption: 3,000 items deep: every new request waits 30 seconds.

steps.title: Work nobody is waiting for
steps.body: Say the spike ends and arrivals fall back to 80 per second, but the 3,000-item backlog remains. Clients, proxies and impatient users often give up after about 5 seconds. A request that waited 30 seconds was abandoned before a worker started it, yet the worker still does the full work and the answer is thrown away. Workers stay 100% busy but almost nothing useful comes out. Draining 3,000 items at a net 20 per second (100 out minus 80 in) takes 150 seconds. Workers can check each request's deadline and skip expired ones, one more reason to keep queues short.
steps.idea: Long queues make workers burn capacity on stale requests, so overload outlasts the spike that caused it.
steps.caption: Stale requests reach workers after clients gave up.

steps.title: Bound the queue
steps.body: Cap the queue at 200 items. At 100 requests per second that is at most 2 seconds of wait, inside the caller's 5-second timeout. When the queue is full, new requests get an immediate 503 or 429 error instead of a slow death. This is backpressure: the system pushes the overload signal back to the sender, which can slow down, retry later or show a message. Other forms make the sender wait instead, like a blocked write on a full buffer or a shrinking TCP window.
steps.idea: A bounded queue caps latency and turns overload into a fast, explicit error callers can react to.
steps.caption: Queue full at 200: excess requests are refused instantly.

steps.title: Shed the least important work
steps.body: Rejecting at random hurts checkout as much as a nightly report. So tag requests with a priority. Say 50 of the 150 requests per second come from batch jobs. The gateway rejects those first and keeps interactive traffic flowing. Batch work can wait or retry in an hour, while a shopper who sees an error leaves. This is load shedding: deliberately dropping some work to protect the rest.
steps.idea: Shedding by priority spends the unavoidable loss on the work that matters least.
steps.caption: Batch requests get 503; interactive requests go through.

steps.title: Reject early, reject cheaply
steps.body: Admission control means deciding at the front door, before any real work starts. A rejection costs almost nothing. A request that is queued and then dropped has already used memory, a connection and maybe a database call. The gate can look at queue depth, number in flight, or the age of the oldest item, and aim for a wait target such as 500 ms. A Retry-After header tells polite clients when to come back.
steps.idea: The cheapest place to say no is before the request enters the system.
steps.caption: The gateway keeps expected wait near 500 ms.

steps.title: Fixed limits go stale
steps.body: A fixed limit is a guess about capacity, and capacity changes. Say a limit of 100 req/s was tuned when 20 workers each took 200 ms per request (20 / 0.2 = 100). Now the database slows to 400 ms, so the same workers finish only 50 req/s. A fixed limit would keep admitting 100. Adaptive concurrency fixes this by limiting requests in flight (concurrency = throughput x latency). It raises the limit slowly while latency is healthy and cuts it sharply, for example by 10% to 50%, when latency rises. Here the in-flight limit stays near 20, so at 400 ms the admitted rate falls to about 50 req/s and the excess is refused.
steps.idea: Adaptive limits follow real capacity by watching latency, instead of trusting a number someone picked last year.
steps.caption: The database slows, so the adaptive limit shrinks to match.

steps.title: Say no early, say no fast
steps.body: Overload is a math problem: when arrivals exceed capacity, something must give. An unbounded queue gives up latency, and eventually the whole service. Bounded queues, priority shedding, admission control and adaptive limits give up a little work on purpose so the rest finishes on time. Clients should treat 429 and 503 as a signal to back off (see the timeouts and retries lesson).
steps.idea: Protect latency by refusing excess work deliberately, early and in priority order.
steps.caption: Fast, explicit rejection keeps the system healthy.

quiz.q: Workers handle 100 requests per second and the queue holds 3,000 items. Roughly how long does a newly accepted request wait?
options: No wait, queues are processed in parallel
quiz.why: Wait is queue length divided by service rate: 3,000 / 100 = 30 seconds, long past most client timeouts.

quiz.q: Why is a bounded queue with fast 503 errors often better than a huge queue that accepts everything?
options: It raises the maximum throughput of the workers
It guarantees no request is ever lost
It removes the need for any timeouts
It caps latency, so accepted requests finish before callers give up and workers avoid stale work
quiz.why: A bound does not add capacity. It keeps waits short so the work done is still useful, and it tells callers early that they should back off.

quiz.q: During overload you must drop 50 req/s. Which approach best fits load shedding?
options: Drop a random 50 req/s across all traffic
Drop batch and background requests first, keep checkout and other interactive traffic
Restart the workers to clear the load
quiz.why: Priority-based shedding spends the unavoidable loss on work that can wait or be retried, protecting the user-facing path.

quiz.q: The database gets twice as slow. Why does an adaptive concurrency limit beat a fixed rate limit of 100 req/s?
options: It lowers the limit when latency rises, matching the reduced real capacity
It always admits more traffic than a fixed limit
It stores requests on disk until the database recovers
quiz.why: A fixed rate limit encodes the old capacity and keeps admitting 100 req/s into a system that can now finish only 50. An adaptive limit watches latency and shrinks, so the excess is refused instead of piling up.

cheatsheet.def: A signal from a slow consumer to its producers to slow down or stop, such as a full queue, a blocked write or a 429 response.
Deliberately dropping some requests under overload so the rest still complete quickly.
Roughly queue length divided by service rate. Keep it well under the caller's timeout.
A queue with a fixed maximum size. When full, new work is rejected instead of buffered forever.
A gate at the entrance that accepts or rejects work based on load signals such as queue depth, in-flight count or oldest item age.
Tagging requests by importance and rejecting low-priority work first, for example batch before interactive.
A limit on in-flight requests that rises slowly while latency is healthy and drops multiplicatively when latency climbs (AIMD style).

429 means this caller is sending too much; 503 means the service is overloaded or unavailable. A per-class shed is sent as 429 if that class has its own quota, 503 if the whole service is overloaded. Both may include Retry-After.
